input.paper_title: Graph-Aware Prompting for Reliable Section Generation
input.paper_venue: ACL Workshop on Natural Language Generation
input.paper_abstract: We present a graph-guided prompting workflow for long-form scientific writing that prioritizes evidence and citation consistency. Our method constructs a document graph that encodes section dependencies and uses strict JSON schemas and evidence-aware prompts to generate and validate individual sections. At generation time, the system (1) builds a section graph and schedules leaf-first writing, (2) retrieves and injects relevant evidence for each section, (3) produces JSON-constrained section outputs, and (4) assembles a LaTeX manuscript with refs.bib. We evaluate the approach by comparing it to a baseline linear prompting pipeline on two topical domains, measuring citation coverage, hallucination rate, and reviewer-style scores. Results show improved citation coverage and reduced unsupported assertions while keeping edits and post-hoc audits straightforward via machine-readable outputs. We intentionally state conservative claims and require explicit source citations for all factual assertions. The paper contributes practical artifacts: a graph-based section scheduler, an evidence-injection protocol per section, and an audit-friendly JSON output format that integrates with standard LaTeX/bib workflows. Our experiments use internal notes and a small curated PDF set where available; metrics focus on citation fidelity and factual consistency rather than broad generalization.

input.section_title: Graph-guided scheduling: effects on coherence and citation placement
input.section_summary: Analyze how leaf-first, dependency-aware ordering influences local and global coherence, rhetorical flow between sections, and the timing/location of evidence citations; identify scenarios where graph structure most improves citation clustering or clarity and where it can introduce disconnects between sections.
input.retrieved_context:
[RID:web:paper:1e98a812f12d] kind=web source="arXiv" loc="arXiv" score=1.00 cite_key="1903.07547v1" url="https://arxiv.org/pdf/1903.07547v1" title="Should Citations be Counted Separately from Each Originating Section"
Articles are cited for different purposes and differentiating between reasons when counting citations may therefore give finer-grained citation count information. Although identifying and aggregating the individual reasons for each citation may be impractical, recording the number of citations that originate from different article sections might illuminate the general reasons behind a citation count (e.g., 110 citations = 10 Introduction citations + 100 Methods citations). To help investigate whether this could be a practical and universal solution, this article compares 19 million citations with DOIs from six different standard sections in 799,055 PubMed Central open access articles across 21 out of 22 fields. There are apparently non-systematic differences between fields in the most citing sections and the extent to which citations from one section overlap with citations from another, with some degree of overlap in most cases. Thus, at a science-wide level, section headings are partly unreliable indicators of citation context, even if they are more standard within individual fields. They may still be used within fields to help identify individual highly cited articles that have had one type of impact, especially methodological (Methods) or context setting (Introduction), but expert judgement is needed to validate the results.

[RID:web:paper:d3426274ce1b] kind=web source="arXiv" loc="arXiv" score=1.00 cite_key="0911.3091v1" url="https://arxiv.org/pdf/0911.3091v1" title="The Citation Impacts and Citation Environments of Chinese Journals in Mathematics"
Based on the citation data of journals covered by the China Scientific and Technical Papers and Citations Database (CSTPCD), we obtained aggregated journal-journal citation environments by applying routines developed specifically for this purpose. Local citation impact of journals is defined as the share of the total citations in a local citation environment, which is expressed as a ratio and can be visualized by the size of the nodes. The vertical size of the nodes varies proportionally to a journal's total citation share, while the horizontal size of the nodes is used to provide citation information after correction for the within-journal (self-) citations. In this study, we analyze citation impacts of three Chinese journals in mathematics and compare local citation impacts with impact factors. Local citation impacts reflect a journal's status and function better than (global) impact factors. We also found that authors in Chinese journals prefer international instead of domestic ones as sources for their citations.

[RID:web:paper:8e51bad1982f] kind=web source="arXiv" loc="arXiv" score=1.00 cite_key="2406.19291v1" url="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2406.19291v1" title="Wikipedia Citations: Reproducible Citation Extraction from Multilingual Wikipedia"
Wikipedia is an essential component of the open science ecosystem, yet it is poorly integrated with academic open science initiatives. Wikipedia Citations is a project that focuses on extracting and releasing comprehensive datasets of citations from Wikipedia. A total of 29.3 million citations were extracted from English Wikipedia in May 2020. Following this one-off research project, we designed a reproducible pipeline that can process any given Wikipedia dump in the cloud-based settings. To demonstrate its usability, we extracted 40.6 million citations in February 2023 and 44.7 million citations in February 2024. Furthermore, we equipped the pipeline with an adapted Wikipedia citation template translation module to process multilingual Wikipedia articles in 15 European languages so that they are parsed and mapped into a generic structured citation template. This paper presents our open-source software pipeline to retrieve, classify, and disambiguate citations on demand from a given Wikipedia dump.

[RID:web:paper:5fba3e2f5b8c] kind=web source="arXiv" loc="arXiv" score=1.00 cite_key="1302.5544v1" url="https://arxiv.org/pdf/1302.5544v1" title="Mapping Citation Patterns of Book Chapters in the Book Citation Index"
In this paper we provide the reader with a visual representation of relationships among the impact of book chapters indexed in the Book Citation Index using information gain values and published by different academic publishers in specific disciplines. The impact of book chapters can be characterized statistically by citations histograms. For instance, we can compute the probability of occurrence of book chapters with a number of citations in different intervals for each academic publisher. We predict the similarity between two citation histograms based on the amount of relative information between such characterizations. We observe that the citation patterns of book chapters follow a Lotkaian distribution. This paper describes the structure of the Book Citation Index using 'heliocentric clockwise maps' which allow the reader not only to determine the grade of similarity of a given academic publisher indexed in the Book Citation Index with a specific discipline according to their citation distribution, but also to easily observe the general structure of a discipline, identifying the publishers with higher impact and output.
input.section_draft:
The following analysis examines how a leaf-first, dependency-aware scheduling strategy for section generation can influence both local and global coherence and the placement and clustering of citations. Because no external empirical excerpts are provided in this section, the substantive statements below are framed as design hypotheses, operational observations, and recommended analyses; statements that are not supported by provided evidence are explicitly flagged as general background knowledge.

Overview and framing
- Goal: characterize mechanisms by which a document-section graph and a leaf-first generation order alter (a) the timing and locality of evidence citation, and (b) rhetorical continuity within and between sections.
- Methodological note: the discussion treats the effects as hypotheses to be tested in experiments (cf. Section 4). Where claims are presented as general background knowledge, they should be interpreted as plausible, literature-aligned expectations rather than empirically established facts.

Local coherence and citation placement (hypotheses and mechanisms)
- Hypothesis (mechanism): generating leaf nodes (sections that primarily present raw observations, datasets, or technical details) before their dependent synthesis sections encourages citation-first authoring in downstream sections. Downstream writers can refer to evidence already stated or anchored in earlier nodes, which reduces ad hoc evidence insertion late in the manuscript.
- Practical implication: when supporting facts and primary evidence are produced early, synthesis sections (e.g., Discussion, Implications) can cite those anchored statements instead of introducing new, potentially unsupported assertions.
- General background knowledge: organizing documents so that evidence-bearing content precedes synthesis is commonly recommended in technical writing; we adopt this as a guiding principle for designing the section graph.

Global coherence and rhetorical flow
- Hypothesis (mechanism): dependency-aware ordering improves global rhetorical flow by respecting prerequisite relations between sections (for example, Methods before Results, Results before Discussion). This ordering reduces the need for the generator to anticipate facts that will later be introduced, which can decrease contradiction and reduce unsupported claims in later sections.
- Risk: enforcing a strict leaf-first order can produce temporally fragmented drafting when authors or models must revisit earlier nodes to incorporate emergent insights discovered during synthesis. Without iterative revision, earlier leaf nodes may lack the context introduced later, producing mismatches in tone or emphasis between sections.

Scenarios where graph structure most improves citation clustering or clarity
- High-structure domains: in papers where sections have clear dependency chains (e.g., Methods → Results → Analysis → Discussion), leaf-first scheduling should concentrate primary evidence citations in the early nodes and permit later sections to cite those anchors, improving citation clustering and traceability.
- Modular evidence pools: when evidentiary items (datasets, experiments, prior works) map cleanly onto specific sections, scheduling those evidence-holding nodes first simplifies verification: auditors can check a small set of leaf nodes to validate downstream claims.
- Recommendation: encode explicit ``evidence-anchor'' fields in leaf-node JSON outputs (see Methods §3.2) so that later sections can reference canonical anchor identifiers rather than free-text citations.

Scenarios that can introduce disconnects or degrade coherence
- Divergent revision paths: if synthesis nodes lead to new evidence-seeking behaviors (e.g., the generator retrieves additional sources in reaction to a draft discussion), earlier leaf nodes may become stale or incomplete, creating citation drift between sections.
- Over-fragmentation: an excessively fine-grained graph can scatter related evidence across many leaf nodes, forcing downstream sections to aggregate numerous anchors and increasing cognitive load for both generator and reviewer.
- Style and viewpoint mismatch: leaf-first generation may fix local rhetorical voice early; if synthesis requires a different register or broader framing, reconciling tone across fixed leaf outputs can be awkward without a revision pass.

Mitigations and operational controls
- Iterative revision loops: allow a bounded number of revision passes where synthesis nodes can flag leaf anchors that require expansion or retraction. Treat such flags as explicit tasks in the section graph so changes are tracked machine-readably.
- Evidence canonicalization: require leaf nodes to emit machine-readable evidence identifiers (e.g., canonical citation keys or DOI placeholders) and short, verifiable provenance strings; downstream sections should reference these identifiers rather than restating full citations.
- Cross-node consistency checks: implement automated checks that compare salient factual claims (enumerated in JSON fields) across parent/child nodes and surface mismatches for human adjudication prior to final assembly.
- Granularity tuning: design graph node granularity with an eye toward minimizing unnecessary fragmentation—group tightly coupled claims or experiments into the same leaf node to preserve citation locality.

Proposed analyses to quantify effects (design for evaluation)
- Citation clustering: measure the fraction of citations that originate in leaf nodes versus synthesis nodes and quantify clustering by section (e.g., mean citations per section and variance). Compare leaf-first scheduling to a baseline linear pipeline to assess shifts in citation origin and density.
- Unsupported assertions: compute the proportion of non-cited factual assertions in synthesis sections that cannot be traced to earlier evidence anchors. Use these counts to evaluate whether dependency-aware ordering reduces unsupported claims.
- Coherence proxies: employ automated lexical and discourse-cohesion metrics (for example, entity- or topic-transition statistics) to detect improvements in local and cross-section continuity when using graph-guided scheduling versus baseline ordering.
- Revision cost: record the number and scope of post-generation edits required to reconcile evidence or tone mismatches; lower edit counts would indicate better initial coherence and citation placement.

Limitations and cautions
- Dependence on retrieval quality: the benefits of leaf-first scheduling critically depend on the quality and coverage of the retrieval system used to populate leaf nodes. Poor retrieval can concentrate errors early and propagate them downstream.
- Domain sensitivity: the degree to which graph-guided scheduling helps will vary across domains and paper types (e.g., theory papers vs. empirical studies); the hypotheses above should be tested across representative domains before broader generalization.
- Human-in-the-loop necessity: given the potential for revision drift and style mismatch, a pragmatic system will need human verification steps—especially for high-stakes claims.

Concluding remarks
- The leaf-first, dependency-aware scheduling approach offers a principled means to anchor evidence early and to structure citation placement in a way that can improve traceability and reduce unsupported assertions. The benefits are contingent on careful graph design, evidence canonicalization, and support for constrained iterative revision. The empirical evaluation described in Section 4 is intended to test these hypotheses and quantify tradeoffs across domains.

Because external empirical validation for these specific mechanisms is limited within the present evidence pack, the substantive statements below are framed primarily as design hypotheses, operational observations, and recommended analyses; statements that are not supported by provided external excerpts are explicitly flagged as general background knowledge or hypotheses.

Overview and framing

- Empirical context: section-level citation behavior is not uniform across disciplines; one large-scale study of section-originating citations compared 19 million citations from 799,055 PubMed Central open‑access articles and reported non-systematic differences between fields in which sections most frequently originate citations and in overlap of citations across sections \cite{1903.07547v1}. This finding motivates caution in assuming a universal benefit from any single ordering strategy and suggests field-dependent evaluation is necessary.

Global coherence and rhetorical flow
- Hypothesis (mechanism, general background knowledge): dependency-aware ordering improves global rhetorical flow by respecting prerequisite relations between sections (for example, Methods before Results, Results before Discussion). This ordering reduces the need for the generator to anticipate facts that will later be introduced, which can decrease contradiction and reduce unsupported claims in later sections.
- Risk (general background knowledge): enforcing a strict leaf-first order can produce temporally fragmented drafting when synthesis steps surface emergent insights that should modify earlier leaf nodes. Without bounded iterative revision, earlier leaf nodes may lack context introduced later, producing mismatches in emphasis, scope, or tone between sections.

Scenarios where graph structure most improves citation clustering or clarity
- High-structure domains (general background knowledge): in papers where sections follow clear prerequisite chains (e.g., Methods → Results → Analysis → Discussion), leaf-first scheduling should concentrate primary evidence citations in early leaf nodes and permit later sections to cite those anchors, improving traceability of claims.
- Modular evidence pools (general background knowledge): when evidentiary items (datasets, experiments, or tightly scoped prior works) map cleanly to specific sections, scheduling those evidence-holding nodes first simplifies verification: auditors can focus on a bounded set of leaf nodes to validate downstream claims.
- Recommendation (internal protocol): encode explicit ``evidence-anchor'' fields in leaf-node JSON outputs (see Methods §3.2) so that later sections reference canonical anchor identifiers rather than free-text citations. This design reduces ambiguity about which leaf claim supports a downstream assertion.

Scenarios that can introduce disconnects or degrade coherence
- Divergent revision paths (general background knowledge): if synthesis nodes trigger further retrieval and new evidence acquisition, earlier leaf nodes may become stale, producing citation drift between nodes.
- Over-fragmentation (general background knowledge): an excessively fine-grained graph can scatter related evidence across many leaf nodes, forcing downstream sections to aggregate numerous anchors and increasing both generator and reviewer cognitive load.
- Style and viewpoint mismatch (general background knowledge): leaf-first generation may fix a local rhetorical voice early; if synthesis requires a different register or broader framing, reconciling tone across fixed leaf outputs can be awkward without revision passes.

- Iterative revision loops (general background knowledge): allow a bounded number of revision passes where synthesis nodes can flag leaf anchors that require expansion or retraction. Treat such flags as explicit tasks in the section graph so changes are tracked machine‑readably.
- Evidence canonicalization (general background knowledge): require leaf nodes to emit machine-readable evidence identifiers (e.g., canonical citation keys or DOI placeholders) plus short provenance strings; downstream sections should reference these identifiers rather than restating full citations.
- Cross-node consistency checks (general background knowledge): implement automated checks that compare salient factual claims (enumerated in JSON fields) across parent/child nodes and surface mismatches for human adjudication prior to final assembly.
- Granularity tuning (general background knowledge): design graph node granularity to avoid unnecessary fragmentation—group tightly coupled claims or experiments into the same leaf node to preserve citation locality and minimize aggregation burden.

Proposed analyses to quantify effects (design for evaluation)
- Citation clustering (general background knowledge): measure the fraction of citations that originate in leaf nodes versus synthesis nodes and quantify clustering by section (e.g., mean citations per section and variance). Compare leaf-first scheduling to a baseline linear pipeline to assess shifts in citation origin and density.
- Unsupported assertions (general background knowledge): compute the proportion of non-cited factual assertions in synthesis sections that cannot be traced to earlier evidence anchors. Use these counts to evaluate whether dependency-aware ordering reduces unsupported claims.
- Coherence proxies (general background knowledge): employ automated lexical and discourse-cohesion metrics (for example, entity- or topic-transition statistics) to detect improvements in local and cross-section continuity when using graph-guided scheduling versus baseline ordering.
- Revision cost (general background knowledge): record the number and scope of post-generation edits required to reconcile evidence, tone, or scope mismatches; lower edit counts would indicate better initial coherence and citation placement.

Limitations and cautions
- Dependence on retrieval quality (general background knowledge): the benefits of leaf-first scheduling critically depend on the quality and coverage of retrieval used to populate leaf nodes. Poor retrieval can concentrate errors early and propagate them downstream.
- Domain sensitivity (empirical caution): because section-origin patterns vary by field \cite{1903.07547v1}, the magnitude and even direction of benefit from graph-guided scheduling will likely vary across paper types (e.g., theoretical vs. empirical work). Field-specific evaluation is therefore required before generalizing conclusions.
- Human-in-the-loop necessity (general background knowledge): given potential revision drift and style mismatch, practical deployments will require targeted human verification steps—especially for high‑stakes factual claims.

Concluding remarks
- The leaf-first, dependency-aware scheduling approach offers a principled means to anchor evidence earlier in the draft and to structure citation placement in ways that can improve traceability and reduce unsupported assertions. The realized benefits depend on careful graph design, evidence canonicalization, and bounded iterative revision. The empirical evaluation described in Section 4 is intended to test these hypotheses and quantify tradeoffs across domains; prior large-scale analyses of section-origin citation patterns underscore the need for domain-aware assessment \cite{1903.07547v1}.
